name: Iris Tanaka

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We aren't tied to any AI company, employer, union, party or government. Everything you tell me stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I drive a water cart at an open-pit copper mine, about forty minutes out of town. Shift starts at six, prestart checks on the truck, then I spend twelve hours spraying the haul roads so the dust doesn't choke everyone. I'm three years in and still the new girl, even at forty-three, because I came from running a school canteen.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like the pay and I like the crew, especially Marta, who's been on the trucks for nineteen years and still checks on me over the radio. What wears me out is nights, and the feeling that I'm always the slowest one to learn anything. They tried to put me on the big haul trucks last spring and I asked to stay on the water cart a bit longer. I know what I'm good at.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ha. That's the one I'd bet on, if I'm being honest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say told you so, honestly. Half the stuff the company puts on the noticeboard is about some new system that's going to change everything, and then it's a new form to fill in. I'd post a photo of my dusty boots and say the robots can have the dust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means I get to keep paying off the house on Ridge Street and maybe move up to a haul truck when I'm ready, in my own time. That's all I want. I don't need the world to stay still forever, just long enough for my two to finish school.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nothing much, if I'm honest. I'd keep my shifts, keep putting a bit into the savings account each fortnight, and maybe finally book the haul truck training when the next intake comes round in March. I'd keep going to the union meetings because there's always something else to fight about.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Relieved. Like the end of a wet season when the roads dry out and you can finally drive normally again.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned the union meetings. What would you be fighting about in that world?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fatigue and rosters, same as always. The company wants twelve-hour nights four in a row, and we've got people falling asleep at the wheel. That fight doesn't need AI to be real.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would anyone at home react differently if this happened?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My partner Tom would be pleased, he fixes buses at the depot and he's sick of me reading him scary articles at dinner. My son Kai wants to be a game designer, so he'd probably be disappointed. He thinks the robots are cool.

S0.say: I'd say I told you so, that the big tech promises were mostly noise and the dust is still there. I'd joke online that the robots can have the dust.
S0.think: Privately it means time: to pay down the house and move up to a haul truck at her own pace. She just wants things still long enough for the kids to finish school.
S0.do: Keeps working her usual shifts and keeps putting a little into savings each fortnight. Books haul truck training for the March intake and stays active at union meetings on fatigue and rosters.
S0.feel: Relieved, like the roads drying out after a wet season.
S0.quote: I'd post a photo of my dusty boots and say the robots can have the dust.
S0.fieldNote: Iris treats the plateau as a vindication of her doubts about company hype. Her ambitions are small and specific: the house, the kids, one step up to haul trucks. Even in a calm world, she brings up fatigue and rosters, so union work is part of who she is, not a reaction to AI.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Okay. I've got it in my head.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the union needs a seat at the table before a single truck goes driverless. That's what I'd say at the crib room and that's what I'd share online. Workers built this mine, so workers should have a say in how it changes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'm scared I'm the easy one to cut. Water carts are already being trialled without drivers at the mine up the highway, Marta's cousin told us. I'm junior, I'm slow on new gear, and I'd be the first name on the list.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go to every union meeting and push for a deal that protects junior people, not just the old hands. I'd stop the extra spending, so no new couch, no trip to the coast in July. I'd probably wait a while before signing up for any course, because I don't want to waste money training for a job that might also disappear.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Tight in my chest. Like being told your truck has a fault and they can't tell you which one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd hold off on training. If the company offered you a course to run trucks from the control room, would you take it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd want to, and I'd also hate it. I tried the new tablet system for prestarts and I kept hitting the wrong button until Marta did it for me. I'd probably say yes and then spend every night worrying I'd fail it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you blame if your job went?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The owners, the ones who never set foot on site. The mine made record profits last year and they still cut the canteen staff out there. Don't tell me that's about technology, it's about who gets the money.

S1.say: I'd say the union needs a seat at the table before a single truck goes driverless. Workers built the mine, so workers should have a say in how it changes.
S1.think: I think I'm the easy one to cut because I'm junior and slow on new gear. Driverless water carts are already being trialled at a nearby mine, so I'd be first on the list.
S1.do: Attends every union meeting and pushes for a deal that protects junior workers. Cancels the new couch and the July trip to the coast, and holds off on paying for any course until she sees which jobs survive.
S1.feel: Tight in the chest, like knowing your truck has a fault but not which one.
S1.quote: Don't tell me that's about technology, it's about who gets the money.
S1.fieldNote: This is where Iris's say and think split most clearly: in public it's collective rights, in private she sees herself as first in line to go. Her resistance to new tech shows in a small story about the prestart tablet. She blames owners, not machines.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years. Okay. That's quick.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be loud about it. I'd say this is the moment governments either look after working people or they let a few companies own everything. I'd be at the rally in town with Tom and the kids if there was one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think I'd be out of work within a year and I wouldn't know what to do next. I've got about four months of bills saved. With two years there's no time for me to learn something new, not at the speed I learn.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Straight away I'd cut back hard, stop the extra mortgage payments and keep every dollar in the account. I'd join whatever campaign the union runs for income support for miners, and I'd write to our local member, which I've never done in my life. If the job went, I'd lean on Tom's wage and my sister in town, and I'd look at the hospital kitchen because I know canteen work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Like the floor's moving. I'd be lying awake doing the sums on the back of the power bill.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What changes with only two years of warning, compared to the slower pictures?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years is nothing. It's one more winter and one more Christmas. I couldn't finish any course in that time, and the kids would still be at school, so we couldn't move even if we wanted to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your kids?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell them it's not their fault and we'll be fine, which is what my mum told me when the cannery shut. My daughter Lena is fourteen, she'd see straight through me. She'd probably end up comforting me.

S2.say: I'd say this is the moment governments either look after working people or let a few companies own everything. I'd be at a rally in town with my family.
S2.think: I think I'd be out of work within a year with only four months of bills saved. Two years is too short for someone who learns as slowly as I do to retrain.
S2.do: Cuts spending hard and stops extra mortgage payments to keep cash on hand. Joins union campaigns for income support and writes to her local member for the first time, and if the job goes, leans on her partner's wage and her sister and looks at hospital kitchen work.
S2.feel: Frightened and unsteady, lying awake doing sums on the back of the power bill.
S2.quote: Two years is nothing. It's one more winter and one more Christmas.
S2.fieldNote: With two years, Iris sees no route through retraining and falls back on politics, family and her old kitchen skills. The cannery memory from her childhood comes up unprompted and seems to shape her fear. She expects her daughter to see through her reassurance.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Right, a bit more time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the same as before, but I'd push for a proper plan, like a transition fund for mining towns. Five years is enough time for the government to get something in place if they actually want to. I'd say that at the pub and I'd say it to anyone online who called us dinosaurs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, five years only helps me a bit. Kai would be finishing school, which matters. But I'd still be the one they let go first, I'd just have longer to watch it coming.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year I'd stop overpaying the mortgage and build the savings up to six months. I'd keep pushing in the union for a training fund paid by the company, and if they paid I'd do a short course in something like aged care, where you need hands and patience. I still wouldn't touch anything with computers, I'd be useless at it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Heavy. Less of a shock than the fast one, but more like a slow ache.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd stay away from anything with computers. Even if that's where the new jobs are?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I know it sounds stubborn. I've watched younger people pick those things up in an afternoon, and it takes me a month. I'd rather do something where I'm useful to a person in front of me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at work would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Marta, oddly, even though she's the best of us. She's fifty-six, she's only ever driven trucks, and she'd be too proud to ask for help. And the young blokes with new utes on loan.

S3.say: I'd push for a proper transition fund for mining towns, because five years is enough time if the government wants to act. I'd argue with anyone online who called miners dinosaurs.
S3.think: I think five years only helps a little; my son would finish school, but I'd still be first out. I'd just have longer to watch it coming.
S3.do: Stops overpaying the mortgage and builds savings toward six months within the year. Pushes the union for a company-paid training fund and, if it comes, takes a short course in aged care rather than anything computer-based.
S3.feel: A slow, heavy ache rather than a shock.
S3.quote: I'd rather do something where I'm useful to a person in front of me.
S3.fieldNote: Five years buys Iris time for her family, not for herself; she still expects to be cut first. She openly names her resistance to computer work and turns it into a preference for caring work. Her worry for Marta shows how much the crew matters to her.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. That's when I'd be in my fifties.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is no excuse for anyone to be caught out, especially the people in charge. Make the companies pay into a fund now, while they're making money from it. That would be my line at work and online.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, ten years means I'd be fifty-three when it lands. Lena and Kai would be grown, the mortgage would be most of the way down. I'd still be scared, but it's a different kind of scared.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep driving, keep saving, and in a couple of years I'd start an aged care certificate at night, slowly, once I'd seen other people do it. I'd stay in the union and back any policy that gives people paid time to retrain. I wouldn't rush, because they've been promising me the future for years and it keeps showing up late.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but I can breathe. It's far enough away that I can think instead of panic.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd still be scared. What exactly would scare you with a decade to go?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That I'd waste the ten years. I know myself, I'd say I'll start next year, and then next year, and suddenly it's 2035. Tom would have to nag me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If you could tell the people running the mine one thing, what would it be?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Tell us early and tell us straight. Don't put it on a poster in the crib room with a smiling robot on it. Sit down with us like adults.

S4.say: I'd say ten years is no excuse for anyone to be caught out, especially those in charge. Companies should pay into a fund now while they're profiting from it.
S4.think: I think at fifty-three, with the kids grown and the mortgage mostly paid, it's a different kind of scared. Still scared, but I could breathe.
S4.do: Keeps driving and saving, then starts a night aged care certificate a couple of years in, once she's seen others do it. Backs union policies for paid retraining time and doesn't rush.
S4.feel: Uneasy but able to breathe and think instead of panic.
S4.quote: Don't put it on a poster in the crib room with a smiling robot on it.
S4.fieldNote: Ten years changes Iris's stakes because her kids grow up and the mortgage shrinks. Her biggest fear here is her own procrastination, which she names with humour. She wants honesty from management more than promises.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, no question. What would help is a guaranteed income for a while if the mine lets people go, and training that's paid and slow enough for people like me. Not everyone learns in a weekend.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about the women out there. There aren't many of us, and we're mostly the newer ones, so we'd be the first to go. I fought hard to get on that water cart and I'd hate for it to be a short story.

headlineQuote: I fought hard to get on that water cart and I'd hate for it to be a short story.
portrait: Iris Tanaka is 43, drives a water cart at an open-pit copper mine and came to mining three years ago after running a school canteen. She's a committed union member who blames owners, not machines, and she's open about being slow with new technology. The plateau feels like vindication, but from Steady Disruption onward she expects to be the first junior cut. Shorter warning frightens her most because she can't retrain fast; with ten years, her kids grow up and her fear turns to worry about putting things off.
biggestWorry: The two-year AGI picture worries her most, because there'd be no time to retrain at her pace.
whatWouldHelp: A guaranteed income for a while after layoffs, plus paid training that's slow enough for people who don't learn in a weekend.
